pedagogy.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D↔3-D relationship. It is best taught by having children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, and verify by folding — then check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close (gaps or overlaps) turns errors into structural learning.
bestPractices: Construct-then-fold-to-verify; have the child predict the solid before folding rather than assembling by trial and error.
Start from a base face and add faces in composites; include tabs for assembly so the model closes cleanly.
Check the count: the built solid's faces, edges and vertices should match the target (a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
Compare several valid nets for the same solid and diagnose why a non-closing net fails — is it the face-set or the arrangement?
keyRepresentations: Card or Polydron nets folded into solids
A tabbed net template that folds and tapes shut
The triangular-prism net: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles forming a band
Base-face-plus-composite layout (band of rectangles, then the two ends)
commonMisconceptions: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid.
Chooses the wrong face-set (e.g. all rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles for a prism).
Arranges the correct faces so the net cannot close; blames ragged cutting rather than the layout.

learn.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D to 3-D relationship. Children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, then fold to verify and check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites (e.g. a band of rectangles plus two triangular ends) reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close — gaps or overlaps — turns errors into structural learning. The worked example throughout is the triangular prism: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles, with 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

activities.title: Construct and fold the net of a triangular prism
feedback: Before folding, ask: which rectangle is the base, and how will each face meet its neighbours when folded? A band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end is one reliable layout to start from. Other valid layouts exist, such as one with a rectangle attached to a triangle, so test the fold rather than rejecting a net only because it has no band.

If a triangle is left flapping, or a gap remains even though the pieces were cut accurately, check two things. First, the layout: will each face meet its neighbour when folded? If not, try redrawing from the band-plus-ends composite. Second, the measurements: each triangle side should equal the width of the rectangle it joins, and all rectangles should have the same length. If the net itself is correct but only the cutting or taping is ragged, provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the layout reasoning rather than scissor control.

When counting, prompt: how many corners does each triangular end have? So how many vertices altogether? How many edges are on each triangular end, and how many edges join the two ends? Check the totals against 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.
If the child reproduces a familiar cube 'cross' net, unfold a real triangular prism to reveal its actual net and contrast the two.
activities.rationale: The procedure ends in a genuinely 3-D solid, so folding the net up and rotating the sealed shape to count faces, edges and vertices is the target skill. Successful builders anchor imaged folding to a base face and known composites; diagnosing why a net won't close moves children from judging by appearance to reasoning about structure.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Using card, a ruler and scissors, draw the net of a triangular prism: two congruent triangles and three rectangles of equal length, each rectangle as wide as the triangle side it joins.
Before cutting, predict and say which shape will be the bottom (base) and which two shapes will cap the ends.
Cut out the net, fold along the edges and tape it shut.
Point to the finished solid and count its faces, edges and vertices (target: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: A valid net is more than the right set of faces — the faces must be arranged so they fold into a closed solid, and the structure of that solid (faces, edges, vertices) can be read off the built 3-D shape rather than the flat drawing.

activities.title: Drag-to-build a net and predict the fold
feedback: On folding, flag gaps, overlaps and any face left flapping so the child can see exactly where the layout fails.
Immediate close/fail feedback on the fold doubles as a check of the construction procedure.
A flat on-screen view slightly under-sells the real 3-D fold, so confirm the count on a rotatable solid or a physical model.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-build editor with a fold animation and immediate close/fail feedback exercises the construction procedure and lets children test many layouts quickly. It is offered as a supplement to physical construction, not a replacement; a flat screen view represents, rather than replaces, the 3-D fold. Efficacy relative to physical building is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Drag two triangles and three rectangles onto a grid to lay out a candidate net.
State which solid you predict it will make and which faces will be the base and the ends.
Fold the layout and watch how the rectangles and triangles move. Check whether every face meets its neighbour so the ends are capped and the prism closes.

If a face is left flapping or a gap or overlap appears, rearrange the faces so they meet correctly, for example by re-anchoring on a band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end, then fold again.
Rotate the sealed solid and tap round it to tally faces, edges and vertices.
activities.intendedInsight: A layout that 'looks fine' flat may still fail to close. Checking how each face will meet its neighbours when folded is what shows whether the prism seals. A band of three rectangles with triangular ends is one dependable layout, but not the only valid one.

activities.title: Compare and diagnose nets for the same solid
feedback: If the child counts wrong faces (e.g. four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles), hand them the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before deciding; count faces first.

For an arrangement failure, have the child trace which edges will meet when folded and find where faces overlap or leave a gap. Rearranging into a band of three rectangles between the two triangular ends is one reliable fix, though not the only valid net.
A sorting task like this can check and build classification of nets, but it does not itself elicit independent construction of a net from scratch; use it alongside, not instead of, building.
activities.rationale: Comparing valid nets and diagnosing why a non-closing net fails separates face-set errors from arrangement errors and builds the structural scheme. Coordinating spatial visualisation with property-based reasoning is what lets children see past the 'look' of the flat drawing.
sourceClaims: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D representation, which is why some children build by appearance rather than structure.
learnerActions: Given several candidate nets for a triangular prism, sort them into those that will fold shut and those that will not.

For each failing net, say whether the problem is the face-set (wrong shapes, wrong number or mismatched sizes) or the arrangement (correct faces placed so that, when folded, some overlap or leave a gap).
Find two different valid nets for the same prism and explain why both work.
Reason about a near-miss: if a net has three triangles and two rectangles, could it fold into this prism, or into any closed solid at all? Explain using the faces a triangular prism needs.
activities.intendedInsight: Nets fail for two distinct reasons — the wrong set of faces, or a correct set arranged so it cannot close — and the same solid can have more than one valid net.

constraints: A static exploded or net diagram (even one tagged face-to-face, or where tapping a net face shows where it lands on the solid) is a useful planning reference but does not enact the fold-and-check procedure; use it to support planning, not as the build itself.
Matching or sequencing tasks that pair solids to nets and counts check recognition of nets and counts but do not elicit independent construction of a net; use them as a post-check.
Discussion can prompt a prediction for the child to justify, but talking does not itself elicit the physical construction and folding that is the target skill.
When cutting, folding or taping leaves ragged gaps, the fold-check becomes inconclusive — provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning rather than scissor control.
A flat 2-D interactive represents the 3-D fold and may under-sell it; confirm face/edge/vertex counts on a rotatable or physical solid.
Include assembly tabs so the model closes cleanly.

Building simple 3-D shapes, including making nets, is part of the Key Stage 2 (Year 6) national curriculum for England. Physical construction with card, ruler and scissors is the core experience in this guidance; digital editors are a supplementary option, not a replacement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the triangular prism: 2 triangular faces + 3 rectangular faces = 5 faces; 3 edges on each triangular end (6) + 3 connecting edges = 9 edges; 3 vertices on each triangular end = 6 vertices. These match the source values (5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).

The near-miss prompt (three triangles and two rectangles) is retained as a reasoning probe: that face-set does not form a triangular prism, so the expected answer is 'no'. Kept as a diagnostic question, not as a construction instruction.

The legacy row ranked a 3-D interactive as 'ideal' and a conversation as 'poor'. Comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the cited sources, so artefacts are presented as options with stated affordances and limits rather than universal claims.

The National Curriculum claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims because that activity's rationale concerns a teaching principle (imaged folding/structure) rather than the curriculum objective itself; the curriculum requirement is retained as a constraint and in the audit.

probeDeeper: Before you fold — which shape will be the bottom, and which two will be the ends?
Your model has a gap here. Is the net wrong, or the way it is arranged? Show me.
How many edges meet at that top corner? So how many vertices altogether?
If I gave you a net with three triangles and two rectangles, what solid would that build — could it be this prism?
assess.correctAnswer: Draws a net of two congruent triangles and three rectangles positioned so the rectangles form a band that wraps between the triangular ends; folds it to a closed prism with no gaps or overlaps; and, pointing to the built solid, counts 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices — self-correcting the layout if a first attempt won't close.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong faces for the solid — e.g. draws four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles, for a triangular prism
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand the child the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before drawing; count faces first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The net has too few or too many faces, or the wrong shapes, and won't wrap between the two triangular ends

errorPatterns.pattern: Places the correct faces in an arrangement that cannot fold shut — the three rectangles don't form a continuous band, so the ends never meet
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor a base rectangle, fold the band of three rectangles first, then attach the two triangular ends; re-draw from that composite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Folding leaves a gap or overlap; the child blames the cutting rather than the layout

errorPatterns.pattern: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unfold a real triangular prism to reveal its actual net and contrast it with the cube net
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attempts a cross of six shapes regardless of the target prism

errorPatterns.pattern: Has the right net but cutting, folding or taping leaves gaps, so the fold-check is inconclusive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning, not scissor control
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The net is correct on paper but the model is ragged and the child is unsure whether it 'worked'

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a net that closes into the target solid; reproduces a memorised cube net or an unfoldable arrangement.
responseLevels.full: Constructs a valid net by choosing the right faces and arranging them as a band-plus-ends composite, folds to a closed solid, self-corrects a faulty layout, and reads faces, edges and vertices off the 3-D structure.
responseLevels.partial: Builds the solid when given a correct net or after trial and error and counts faces, but cannot construct a valid net from scratch or explain why an arrangement fails — parts without structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is card, a ruler, and scissors. Construct the net of a triangular prism, then fold and tape it to check it makes the solid. When it is built, tell me how many faces, edges and vertices it has by pointing to them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child build separates those holding a structural scheme (base band plus two ends, faces in the right composite) from those assembling by trial and error or reproducing a memorised cube net. A wrong face-set or a net that won't close is visible immediately, and the face/edge/vertex count exposes whether the child reads the 3-D structure rather than the flat drawing.
